newsitem.title: USA: Dollar begins US mixed, tests lows versus yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar begins US mixed, tests lows versus yen.

text.p: The dollar began U.S. trade mixed on Friday, holding just above session lows against the yen, but garnering a decent bid versus the mark to debut near the 1.70 threshold.

Short-covering in Asia pushed dollar/yen as high as 117, where offers emerged. Reports that the Bank of Japan was not concerned about the dollar's recent retreat accelerated the push lower, but dealers predicted good interest to buy dollars near the 115 level.

"We had a very difficult time getting through 115 yen on the move up and some people are thinking that this 114.70 low we saw (Thursday) could be a bottom for the time being," said James Powers, vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
The dollar opened at 115.35/45 yen, down from 115.75/85 at Thursday's close. Shortly after the beginning of U.S. trade the dollar poked below 115 yen to test Thursday's four-and-a-half month low.
The greenback began at 1.7000/05 marks, up from 1.6965/70 on Thursday.

Dealers expected the dollar to remain well-bid against Europe, and the mark in particular, which sunk to its lowest level against the yen since September 1995 on Friday. In early U.S. dealings, mark/yen was at its low for the day of 67.73.
"I think the thing that you have to keep you're eye on is dollar/Swiss holding above 1.4250 and dollar/mark above 1.6940," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank.
"On the close that would be slightly dollar bullish and I think dollar/yen could go on the upside in sympathy if we can clear 116.30 on the close today."
Keeping the dollar in check on Friday was uncertainty ahead of next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

The foreign exchange market remains divided on whether the Fed will push rates higher for a second consecutive meeting, although the consensus has moved toward steady policy in the wake of recent subdued data on inflation and industrial output.
A solid 2.6 percent rise in U.S. April housing starts on Friday was seen as evidence of continued strong economic growth, but was unlikely to sway the Fed in one direction or the other, dealers said.
They predicted more consolidation at the dollar's lower levels and said significant further damage was unlikely regardless of the Fed's decision next week.

"I think we have fair value here in the dollar, we've seen a nice correction especially in dollar/yen, and long term fundamentals are still indicative of a higher dollar over the medium term," said Sumitomo's Gariano.

Elsewhere, on Friday, the Bank of Spain reduced its key money market rate to 5.25 from 5.50 percent after data earlier in the week showed Spanish inflation had fallen to 1.7 percent in April -- its lowest level in nearly three decades.
The move had little impact on mark/Spain which was changing hands at 84.26/28 in early U.S. dealings.

German plans to revalue its gold reserves continued to reverberate throughout Europe on Friday, generating criticism from EU partners, but having little tangible impact on the mark, according to traders.
In other trade, the dollar opened flat at 1.4280/90 Swiss francs and retreated to Canadian $1.3669/74 from C$1.3709/14 on Thursday.
Sterling opened lower at $1.6390/00 versus $1.6428/38 and the Australian dollar opened at $0.7749/54, down from $0.7770/75.
